We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.
item.dc:creator: Qiwei Wu, Xiangyu Chen, Xin Xiang, Rui Zhang, Yihang Kang, Weiran Chen, Zikang Xie, Yangfan Li, Tao Wang, Xiangzheng Wang, Tianyi Bi, Zhiyan Zhang, Xianpeng Wang, Mingqian Zhou, Yan Yu, Chuanyu Li, Wenjie Zhang, Tao Li, Weihua Zhang, Renjing Xu, Junjie Lai

item.title: $\zeta_0$: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.29277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $\zeta_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $\zeta_0$ built on $\Psi_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/
item.dc:creator: Yizhi Chen, Zhanxiang Cao, Yitong Wang, Junyu Liu, Hongchu Zeng, Xinyi Peng, Chuxuan Huang, Yicheng Su, Zihao Zhou, Shengcheng Fu, Haoyang Li, Liyun Yan, Tianyue Zhan, Jianming Ma, Yang Zhang, Keqi Zhu, Xiaxi Si, Jinming Yao, Qiao Sun, Shizeng Zhang, Jiangwei Zhong, Yue Gao

item.title: A2I-VLA: A Two-Stage Vision-Language-Action model with Semantic-Physical Alignment and Integration
item.description: arXiv:2611.29279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.
item.dc:creator: Kun Dai, Tianqi Wang, Haibo Lei, Chaoyang Li, Kai Zhang, Fuyuan Qiu, Lijun Zhao, Ruifeng Li, Chuqing Cao, Tao Xie, Wenming Tan

item.title: RSLaA: Self-Reconfiguring Roadside LiDARs as Agents for 3D Traffic Perception
item.description: arXiv:2611.29294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because infrastructure deployment is costly, existing work optimizes RSL configurations once, against road geometry and aggregated traffic statistics, and treats them as fixed thereafter. Traffic flow, however, is inherently dynamic, and a placement optimal on average can be far from optimal at any given moment. We introduce RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows. Since ground truth is unavailable at decision time, the framework centers on surrogate metrics computed solely from a probabilistic occupancy grid of historical observations, which predicts the next-window perception performance of candidate poses. We construct a co-simulation benchmark pairing five candidate surrogates with detector-agnostic ground-truth perception labels at every decision window, identifying the multi-view coverage metric J_mv as the most reliable predictor. Upon this validated surrogate we build two adaptive configuration methods, a receding-horizon (MPC) optimizer and a lightweight MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with centralized training and decentralized execution. Across 10 sites and 89 six-hour traffic scenarios (890 evaluation runs), adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment. Our results indicate that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.
item.dc:creator: Yang Ma, Yichen Sun, Yubing Zheng, Zhongxiang Feng, Zeyang Cheng, Said M. Easa

item.title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.
item.dc:creator: Meng-Hao Guo, Yi Zhang, Zhe-Han Mo, Han-Zheng Wang, Jia-Jun Wang, Xin-Sheng Chen, Jiaxi Song, Yi-Xuan Deng, Jia-Ning Li, Xuanyu Chu, Hengrui Zhang, Huan-ang Gao, Yongming Rao, Shi-Min Hu

item.title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.
item.dc:creator: Xin Zhang, Yushuo Hou, Anqi Zhao, Moyun Liu, Xingwei Zhao, Bo Tao, Jiawei Du, Joey Tianyi Zhou

item.title: Specification-Aware Sparse Differentiation: Planning under Signal Temporal Logic with Sparsemax Robustness
item.description: arXiv:2611.29346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gradient-based optimal control under a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification involves solving a nonlinear program whose constraints are smoothed robustness functions of the trajectory, and automatic differentiation without knowledge of sparsity computes the Jacobian and the Hessian that its solver needs in full. This often renders the problem computationally intractable. The dynamics and the specification prescribe a sparsity pattern through the STL syntax, the windows of the temporal operators and the variables that the predicates read. Standard tools such as CasADi recover this pattern by structural detection. In this work, we propose a method to prescribe such a pattern directly from the task specification. We show that our method allows us to exploit SparseMax, a recently proposed smooth robustness operator that is certifiably sparse and sound. Its derivative is exactly zero at every operand at or below a data-dependent threshold, which structural detection cannot see. We derive the patterns that expose this trajectory-dependent sparsity to sparse automatic differentiation, with a margin test for their reuse and Hessians confined to the variables of each constraint's support. We demonstrate the method on a dual-arm coordination task in which two arms share a hand-off zone divided into cells and one until constraint per scheduled visit keeps the other arm out of a cell until the visitor has left it. The two scenes are a zone of five cells and a circle of 64 cells, with single solves and closed-loop re-planning on a rigid-body simulation. Our exact-Hessian interior-point solves are up to 27 times faster than those with the sound log-sum-exp robustness in CasADi and IPOPT.
item.dc:creator: Sai Sandeep Damera, Ryan Matheu, John S. Baras, Calin Belta

item.title: Contact Harness: Enabling VLM Agents to Perform Contact-Rich Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force and tactile feedback provide complementary information, but their semantic ambiguity makes them difficult for agents to use directly. These signals must be interpreted according to their physical meaning, together with task phase and visual evidence. We propose Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions. A compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback. The framework requires no model fine-tuning, task demonstrations, or simulation training. We conduct zero-shot real-robot evaluations using GPT-6 Astra on Rokae and Franka robots. With a single prompt skill, Contact Harness achieves a full-insertion rate of 90.7% across 15 connector types, with further evaluations on a real PC under variations in lighting, background, and position. Across four additional contact-rich tasks, including whiteboard wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting, Contact Harness achieves an average success rate of 100%. On six simulated tasks, Contact Harness reaches 96.7% success, compared with at most 68.3% for pretrained VLA baselines fine-tuned on task demonstrations, showing the potential of agent-based manipulation for contact-rich real-world deployment.
item.dc:creator: Shilin Shan, Yuxuan Hu, Chuhao Zhou, Yimeng Dong, Bohan Hou, Jiaqi Bai, Boyu Ma, Jiahua Dong, Jianfei Yang

item.title: Self-Refining VLA Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2611.29383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves iteratively updating random noise, and distinct noise samples from the same state can result in distinct trajectories and task outcomes. Existing test-time scaling methods improve action chunk generation via selection, aggregation, or correction, but commonly require the generation of large ensembles of candidates or the training of an external corrector. We adapt Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, to the robotics domain. We find that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data. Across 400 episodes of LIBERO evaluated using SmolVLA, P&P improves upon the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points. Further, episode-level P\&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure (AUC 0.851).
item.dc:creator: Jeff Duan, Arjun Sharma, Jennifer Cruden, Vansh Tibrewal

item.title: Phase-Conditioned Action Contracts for Auditable Microsurgical Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.29426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxi You, Yiwei Shi, Yanlin Li, Rihui Song, Weibing Li, Kai Huang, Weiru Liu

item.title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.29453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
item.dc:creator: Shuaicheng Niu, Guohao Chen, Kevin Z. Shen, Yunbei Zhang, Peilin Zhao, Yinan Zhang, Cyril Leung

item.title: MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.
item.dc:creator: Chiara Boretti, Philippe Bich, Manuel Morteo, Roberto Tron, John Baillieul

item.title: Representation Alignment Is Only as Good as the Teacher's Behavioral Structure
item.description: arXiv:2611.29483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $\pi_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.
item.dc:creator: Zhengfeiyang Zhang, Haoyuan Chen, Hexin Wang, Hanyu Zhou, Zhenglin Wan, Wangbo Zhao, Pengfei Zhou

item.title: MAWAM: Joint Imagination for Collaborative Robot Manipulation with a Multi-Agent World Action Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.29501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.
item.dc:creator: Rongze Tang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianjie Fang, Ziming Liu, Zhaolu Wang, Ziyou Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Wei Wu, Chen Gao, Yong Li, Zhibo Chen

item.title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.
item.dc:creator: Anubhav Pandey, Harshit Nagpal, Aditya Agarwal, Tejasvi Alladi, Fei Richard Yu

item.title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
item.description: arXiv:2611.29518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Qiu, Zhao Yang, Marek Cygan

item.title: Feedback Completion Certificates for Repeated Dwell Tasks with Time Windows
item.description: arXiv:2611.29525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An inspection robot may owe several measurements at the same station, each with a different window in which a dwell can begin. We ask what a feedback controller must retain about earlier visits to guarantee all remaining deadlines under bounded disturbances. For a common spatial predicate and dwell length, removing redundant windows orders the remaining obligations by both endpoints. On every history without an expired obligation, the served windows form a suffix. One boundary and one capped run length therefore preserve the future satisfaction of the original task. On a verified library of branching motion primitives we use this state to recover a feedback policy. For one task type a scalar threshold per run length suffices, with work linear in the number of listed branches per time layer for fixed dwell. Multiple types require a joint recursion. On a quadrotor inspection library the threshold sweep reduced the cost of constructing a reusable full-domain policy, while a sparse Boolean baseline answered a single initial query faster. In a two-station MuJoCo patrol, three task-aware filters all met every window in twelve paired runs each. Of eight initially certified runs, the completion filter retained the certificate in all eight, compared with three for safety-only filtering.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxun Sun, Yuqi Yang, Senlan Yao, Hengyu Xue, Hongming Fu, Zhimu Zhou

item.title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning
item.description: arXiv:2611.29548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.
item.dc:creator: Jiarui Li, Runyu Zhang, Gioele Zardini

item.title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
item.description: arXiv:2611.29553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
item.dc:creator: Thanish Bolla

item.title: Action Windows Are Inherently Temporal: A Benchmark for Time-Sensitive Robotic Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents have surpassed learned-policy baselines on existing robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, these agents still struggle with time-sensitive everyday tasks that existing benchmarks for VLM agents cover only partially. In these tasks, evolving physical processes create finite windows for successful intervention. These action windows are inherently temporal and impose a shared time budget on decision making and physical execution. Coordinating intervention within this budget requires agents to determine when the window opens. We introduce AWAIT, a simulation benchmark that evaluates task completion within action windows while accounting for decision and execution time. Our evaluation reveals difficulties in recognizing window onset and shows that successive decisions and movements can exhaust an action window even when each decision takes less than the window duration. Project page: https://eyja42.github.io/await-site/.
item.dc:creator: Haoxiang Zhan, Haoqin Hong, Congcong Zhu, Jingrun Chen

item.title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding
item.description: arXiv:2611.29609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
item.dc:creator: Taekyung Kim, Ege Yuceel, Steven Hong, Georgios Fainekos, Dimitra Panagou, Bardh Hoxha

item.title: Dr. Grasp-RL: Diverse and Robust Dexterous Grasping via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.29610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.
item.dc:creator: Kunqi Xu, Xiaokang Sun, Xueyan Zou

item.title: TASC: Time-to-Collision Anticipation and Selective Crowd Attention for Non-Holonomic Service Robots
item.description: arXiv:2611.29637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.
item.dc:creator: Mohammadhossein Malmir, Mohammadali Rahmati, Mohammad Reza Kolani, Alois Knoll

item.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_0,\pi_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
item.dc:creator: Jiyong Kwon, Yikun Bai, Amirhossein Mollaali, Guang Lin

item.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.29662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Siyeon Kim, Mohanraj Devendran Shanthi, Joseph C. Liechty, Tucker Hermans

item.title: SparQ4D: Learning to Act through Sparse 4D Queries
item.description: arXiv:2611.29682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces \method, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, \method achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.
item.dc:creator: Siyuan Xie, Jinxi Xiao, Ran Ji, Yikai Liu, Mingxi Li, Xuebing Li, Ye Shi, Yuxiang Gao, Jiayuan Gu

item.title: Performance Evaluation of Nonlinear Model Predictive and Sliding Mode Controllers on a 4-Cable Spatial CSPR in Simscape
item.description: arXiv:2611.29748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR) actuated by four cables. The robot is modeled in two parallel ways: (i) via an analytical dynamic model with included cable elasticity and frictional losses, and (ii) in MATLAB Simscape Multibody, capturing realistic physical effects. Both controllers are implemented under identical reference trajectories, system constraints, and tuning strategies. Our results show that NMPC achieves superior tracking accuracy and stronger disturbance rejection compared to SMC, but at the cost of higher computational demand. Moreover, both controllers were tested on an analytical model of the robot and a Simscape model. The close agreement between the two, for both control schemes, confirms the accuracy of the analytical formulation and its consistency with the physics-based simulation. The study highlights the value of physics-based simulation as a complementary tool for validating advanced controllers under realistic conditions, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.
item.dc:creator: Erfun Bayat Sarmadi, Ali Asadi, Moosa Ayati

item.title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
item.description: arXiv:2611.29749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.
item.dc:creator: Wenjie Lin, Jin Wei-Kocsis

item.title: Into My Arms: Structured reinforcement learning for autonomous transport of objects and humans
item.description: arXiv:2611.29771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms
item.dc:creator: Elle Miller, Reem Almheiri, Takuma Tsukakoshi, Ben Sanati, Tamon Miyake, Yushi Wang, Namiko Saito, Shigeki Sugano, Tetsuya Ogata, Rika Antonova, Oisin Mac Aodha, Sethu Vijayakumar

item.title: Generating Safety-Critical Driving Scenarios from Role-Typed Signal Temporal Logic Specifications Drafted by Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.29800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety-critical scenarios are rare in recorded driving and must be generated to test and train motion planners of automated vehicles. In guided diffusion models, each scenario type needs its own weighted objective, separate from the validity check. Optimized together with the attacker, the vehicle under test can cancel the attack or draw it toward itself. We state each scenario as a signal temporal logic specification with clauses typed by role. Every clause names the agent it may change and the agents it may read, and the vehicle under test reads the attacker only from the attack onset. A large language model drafts the specification from a description, and a type checker accepts it. A compiler derives the optimization: it edits a diffusion model's samples by the smallest change that satisfies the specification, each clause moves only its owner, the attacker is solved against the unreacted vehicle under test before its response, and the monitor of the same specification decides acceptance. On nuScenes and CommonRoad, judged independently of the specification, one parameter set produced valid scenarios at a rate 0.14 above a weighted objective tuned per scenario type, and descriptions yielded at least one valid scenario for 11 of the 16 pre-crash types expressible in the public data. Learned planners fail more often on the generated scenarios than on their seeds. Fine-tuning on them lowers a planner's failure rate on critical scenarios, and the time headway one clause of the label requires, not the generator, sets the size of the gain.
item.dc:creator: Zifan Zeng, Qunli Zhang, Peng Wang, Shiming Liu, Feng Liu, Zheng Hu

item.title: Superellipse Function: A Powerful Geometric Tool for the Design and Deformation Modeling of Tendon-Driven Continuum Manipulators With Flexural Patterns Experiencing Tension Loss
item.description: arXiv:2611.29801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we feature the Superellipse function as a geometric and versatile tool for effective design and modeling of flexural patterns (FPs) in tendon-driven continuum manipulators (TD-CMs) with discontinuous cross section geometries. We also propose a unique complementary mathematical framework and solution algorithm for modeling the effects of distributed and concentrated friction forces- caused by partially-constrained tendons- on tension loss and deformation behavior of a TD-CM designed using a Superellipse function. Particularly, by employing this geometric function, we establish four intuitive functional mappings relating the manipulator's geometric parameters, kinematics, and deformation behavior. Thanks to the features of these intuitive mappings and Superellipse function, we then introduce the concepts of design space and design curve to facilitate intuitive design of a TD-CM with a generic FP geometry experiencing tendon tension loss. To thoroughly evaluate the performance of this novel framework and its aforementioned features, we performed various simulation and experimental studies on TD-CMs designed and fabricated based on a Superellipse function. Results were then analyzed and compared using different error metrics.
item.dc:creator: Yang Liu, Farshid Alambeigi

item.title: How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change?
item.description: arXiv:2611.29818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Wang, Mani Srivastava

item.title: Arcadian: Open-Source Humanoid Ecosystem for Accessible and Customizable Research and Education
item.description: arXiv:2611.29868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reproducing and modifying a meter-scale humanoid remains challenging for research and teaching groups with limited fabrication resources and engineering support. This paper presents Arcadian, an open-source humanoid ecosystem that offers accessible and customizable humanoid hardware and software with community support. Arcadian aims to strike a balance among cost-effectiveness, structural durability, and full customizability, lowering the barrier to entry for research and education. Specifically, this meter-scale humanoid adopts metal-embedded 3D printing to achieve a high strength-to-cost ratio, eliminating the need for computer numerical control (CNC) machining while retaining design flexibility. Extensive simulation and hardware tests validate the design: a reinforcement-learning (RL) locomotion policy trained in simulation transfers to the hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) teleoperation interface drives both arms for simple manipulation tasks. The robot is around one meter tall and costs approximately $6,800 to build. All computer-aided design (CAD) models, the bill of materials, assembly documentation, and training and deployment code are publicly released, distributed through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and supported by a Discord server and a project forum through which community feedback informs design updates. The ecosystem resources are available at https://anonymous-humanoid.gitbook.io/docs.
item.dc:creator: Zelin Shen, Gabriel Ramos Salinas, Qiyu Zhang, Yue Qin, Chen Qian, Yanran Ding

item.title: ProMix: Efficient Data Mixture Optimization for Robotic Imitation via Proxy-Reference DRO
item.description: arXiv:2611.29873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains (-3.8% average and -14.3% worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4% to 76.2%, matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours - versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches - with a +17.1% absolute gain on the worst-case domain.
item.dc:creator: Qie Sima, Wei Xue, Yike Guo

item.title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.29897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138$\times$ while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.
item.dc:creator: Yue Huang, Tianshan Zhang, Zeyu Zhang, Jayeon Kang, Akide Liu, Sungjoon Choi, Dacheng Tao, Hao Tang

item.title: UnderGrasp: Envelopment-Oriented Grasp Refinement for an Underactuated Gripper
item.description: arXiv:2611.29907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Underactuated grippers can form enveloping grasps through passive compliance, while the terminal pose and single width predicted by generic grasp generators do not fully capture the approach-closure process. Conventional collision filtering also struggles to distinguish harmful interference from acceptable contact. We present UnderGrasp, a post-hoc grasp refinement and evaluation framework for an underactuated gripper that reuses grasp candidates and quality priors from a frozen generator. The model jointly encodes the target, local environment, support surface, and approach-path geometry to propose diverse combinations of insertion depth, pre-grasp width, and target closing width for each candidate. These actions are ranked by combining separately predicted envelopment and interaction quality with upstream priors, balancing grasp feasibility, envelopment, and scene disturbance rather than rejecting all environmental contact. The back end is trained solely on configuration and interaction labels generated by gripper-specific simulations, without real-robot grasp labels. Real-robot experiments with an underactuated gripper show that UnderGrasp improves the overall success rate (SR) and the envelopment rate (ER) among successful grasps from 0.55/0.12 to 0.82/0.55 with AnyGrasp, and from 0.42/0.08 to 0.65/0.36 with GraspNet. In contrast, increasing the fixed insertion depth to 40 mm improves ER to 0.35 but reduces SR to 0.52, supporting the value of adaptive refinement. For trials involving target or environmental contact during approach, the conditional success rates increase from 0.36 to 0.89 and from 0.25 to 0.86, respectively, demonstrating more reliable execution under contact. Project page: https://dishenliu2004-hub.github.io/undergrasp-site/
item.dc:creator: Zhiwen Song, Ruidi Liu, Guanglu Jia, Zuowei Chen, Hao Wen, Qing Shi

item.title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.29912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.
item.dc:creator: Jiarui Guo, Jinkai Zhang, Yuanhong Yu, Yongchen Zai, Futang Zhu, Ruizhen Hu, Sida Peng, Xiaowei Zhou

item.title: MoMa-NMP: Scene-Scale Neural Motion Planning for Mobile Manipulators
item.description: arXiv:2611.29913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. We train MoMa-NMP on these demonstrations through behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation, achieving 87.0% success on our simulation benchmark and 77.5% across 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.
item.dc:creator: Adam Kan, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Jiahui Yang, Kenneth Shaw, Deepak Pathak

item.title: TidyFlow: Geometry-Aware Tabletop Arrangement Generation with Human-Aligned Tidiness Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.29918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating tidy tabletop arrangements that align with human organizational preferences requires considering both functional relationships among objects and geometric constraints within limited tabletop space. We present TidyFlow, a tabletop arrangement generation framework that integrates conditional Flow Matching with topology-aware geometric refinement. We construct two tabletop arrangement datasets based on functional grouping and geometric constraints, namely General Tabletop Layouts (GTL) and Workstation Tabletop Layouts (WTL), and introduce a six-dimensional tidiness scoring function. Conditional Flow Matching is employed to learn a multimodal distribution of target arrangements conditioned on object attributes and tabletop geometry. To address geometric errors in generated layouts, we construct topology-aware refinement data based on collision and boundary-violation patterns, and employ a pair-aware attention network to iteratively refine object poses. Experiments demonstrate that, after three refinement iterations, TidyFlow improves geometric validity from 23.21% to 88.91% on GTL and from 10.58% to 57.91% on WTL. Furthermore, a human preference study demonstrates a positive correlation between the proposed tidiness scores and human rankings, achieving a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.5543.
item.dc:creator: Jiahui Qian, Tiandong Wang, Shubao Fan, Chenyu Niu, Erqi Wu

item.title: SAGE-Drive: Benefit-Aware Adaptive Reasoning for Autonomous Driving Planning
item.description: arXiv:2611.29947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning. First, paired planning outcomes with and without explicit reasoning are analyzed to measure the reasoning benefit, i.e., the reduction in planning error achieved by explicit reasoning, which serves as the supervision label. SAGE-Drive then learns to predict these benefits using geometric features of the initial trajectory planned without reasoning and multimodal scene information, and invokes explicit reasoning only for the scenarios with the highest predicted benefits under a predefined reasoning budget. Experiments on 1,497 paired driving scenarios reveal that explicit reasoning improves planning accuracy in 53.5% of cases while degrading it in 46.5%, yielding a near-zero average benefit. On the test set, with a 20% reasoning budget, SAGE-Drive achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 1.5191 m, compared with 1.5252 m for random selection. At a 35% budget, it achieves an ADE of 1.5148 m, close to the 1.5141 m obtained when reasoning is applied to every scenario. These findings establish the predicted reasoning benefit as an effective criterion for reasoning selection, allowing explicit reasoning to be invoked where it improves planning accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Donglei Rong, Wenbin Yao, Congcong Bai, Xi Gao, Qiaoqiao Ren, Sheng Jin, Cheng Xu

item.title: TeleMultiStream: An Integrated Robot Teleoperation System with Low-Latency Multi-Stream Video Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.29980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training embodied-intelligence models requires large-scale, high-quality demonstration data. Robot teleoperation provides an important means of collecting these data. Low-latency teleoperation also helps human operators take control promptly and provide corrective demonstrations in DAgger-based interactive learning. This paper presents TeleMultiStream, a robot teleoperation system that combines multi-stream WebRTC video feedback with UDP pose downlink. The system supports heterogeneous video sources and uses buffer reuse, bounded queues, and native XR rendering to reduce processing and waiting. In wired-LAN ZED Mini tests, TeleMultiStream's software and high-performance hardware encoding modes achieved dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass latency medians of 60 and 66~ms, respectively. These medians were 26.8\% and 19.5\% lower than the 82-ms RobotVision-PC reference, respectively. At the lower tested resolutions, the two TeleMultiStream encoding modes provided comparable visual latency. Their respective medians in three-stream Configuration~1 were 72 and 66~ms. In the higher-resolution Configuration~2, high-performance hardware encoding outperformed software encoding in latency and CPU utilization. It reduced mean encoding time from 11.85 to 8.80~ms and the dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass median from 94 to 88~ms. Its CPU utilization was approximately 67\%, compared with 265\% for software encoding. During three-stream reception with high-performance hardware encoding, the mean corrected one-way UDP latencies at 100~Hz were 1.576 and 1.800~ms in Configurations~1 and~2, respectively. Mean estimated packet loss was 0.0033\% in both configurations. These results support responsive teleoperation for robot demonstration collection.
item.dc:creator: Chenchen Lv, Lingchen Hu, Yaosai Zhang, Chunlan Li, Gengkui Wei, Wei Xin, Li Li

item.title: One Latent World for Heterogeneous LiDARs: A Scan Pattern Agnostic 4D World Model via Direct Ray Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.30007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LiDAR world models generate and predict metric 3D observations in the form of LiDAR scans. They typically synthesize scans following the scan pattern of their training sensor or render them from an intermediate 3D surface or field. However, following one scan pattern limits transfer to LiDARs with other patterns, and rendering from intermediate geometry can cause incorrect depths and false returns. In this paper, we propose a scan pattern agnostic 4D LiDAR world model that decouples the scene from sensor observation, so one spatial latent can be observed by heterogeneous LiDARs at the same mounting position without regeneration. Our decoder predicts the hit probability and depth of each ray directly from the latent, combining global scene context with local features retrieved at a preliminary depth. Without an intermediate surface or field, it reduces incorrect depths and false returns, and as each ray is decoded independently from one latent, LiDARs that share a ray receive the same return and observe one consistent scene. Finally, a diffusion transformer generates scenes in this latent and predicts 4D sequences from observed latents warped by the given ego and object motion. On KITTI-360 and nuScenes, our model generates realistic scenes and reduces the registration error between predicted frames by about 70% relative to the best compared world model. Its decoder yields 19 to 28% lower depth error than the rendering used by other world models, and generated scans benefit several downstream tasks. Our code will be open-sourced. More details are available at https://minwoo0611.github.io/OneLatentWorld.
item.dc:creator: Minwoo Jung, Dongjae Lee, DongGuw Lee, Yeong Sang Park, Maurice Fallon, Ayoung Kim

item.title: FlexWAM: Learning Flexible Visual Routing for World Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.30024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Mingyu Mei, Haojie Xu, Zibo Dai, Hongjie Fang, Shirun Tang, Zhengrui Lv, Yang Liu, Chen Guang, Xingyue Zhao, Huiliang Shen, Zaixing He

item.title: Design of a Compact Cable-driven 4-DoF Salamander Robotic Limb with Large Range of Motion and High Load Capacity
item.description: arXiv:2611.30026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A compact yet agile and powerful limb is essential for amphibious legged robots that transition between spine-based swimming and leg-based terrestrial walking, as salamanders do. Salamander limbs combine large ranges of motion (ROM), multiple degrees of freedom (DoFs), and high load capacity. These features enable swinging and body-weight support during walking, as well as folding alongside the body during swimming. Their proximal kinematics can be represented by three rotational DoFs at the hip and one at the knee. Replicating these capabilities within a compact robotic limb is challenging with direct-drive architectures, because multiple joint-mounted actuators must be sufficiently spaced or placed distally to avoid self-collision, increasing limb size and rotational inertia. Here we present a cable-driven 4-DoF salamander robotic limb with a spatial cable-routing architecture that relocates actuators proximally while preserving large ROM and load capacity. Transmission-induced coupling is mitigated by mechanically compensating multi-segment cable paths, model-based feedforward decoupling, and output-side joint angle feedback. Compared with a direct-drive limb, the proposed design reduces mass by 20.4%, projected envelope area by 20.5%, and estimated effective yaw-axis inertia by 31.9%. Experiments verify independent, decoupled control over joint-angle ranges of 45 deg, 118 deg, 118 deg, and 135 deg for hip pitch, yaw, roll, and knee flexion/extension, respectively. During lifting tests, the limb supported an equivalent vertical load of at least 5.4 times its own weight. The proposed limb provides a compact, biologically representative platform for future studies of salamander locomotion and neural control.
item.dc:creator: Zhuowen Li, Qiyuan Fu, Auke Ijspeert

item.title: Spiking World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/
item.dc:creator: Mingquan Liu, Peng Zhou, Shanming Yao, Shuai Wang, Simo Wu, Malu Zhang

item.title: RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?
item.description: arXiv:2611.30047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.
item.dc:creator: Yunbei Zhang, Yuyou Zhang, Janet Wang, Ming Liu, Yijiang Li, Yikai Wang, Weirui Ye, Ding Zhao, Jihun Hamm

item.title: HERO: Hierarchical Region-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.30072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous exploration is widely used to map unknown environments, yet maintaining both path efficiency and low online computation remains difficult as environment scale increases. Hierarchical planners reduce global search through coarse regional representations but often rely on handcrafted local viewpoint-selection rules.
