item.title: Autonomous UAV Navigation in an Unknown Environment via Multi-Trajectory Model Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.30463v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A novel model predictive control (MPC) formulation, named multi-trajectory MPC (mt-MPC), is presented and applied to the problem of autonomous navigation of an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) in an unknown environment. The UAV is equipped with a LiDAR sensor, providing only a partial description of the surroundings and resulting in time-varying constraints as the vehicle navigates among the obstacles. The control system layout is hierarchical: the low-level loops stabilize the vehicle's trajectories and track the set-points commanded by the high-level, mt-MPC controller. The latter is required to plan the UAV trajectory trading off safety, i.e. to avoid collisions with the uncertain obstacles, and exploitation, i.e. to reach an assigned target location. To achieve this goal, mt-MPC considers different future state trajectories in the same Finite Horizon Optimal Control Problem (FHOCP), enabling a partial decoupling between constraint satisfaction (safety) and cost function minimization (exploitation). Recursive feasibility and, consequently, persistent obstacle avoidance guarantees are derived under the assumption of a time invariant environment. The performance of the approach is studied in simulation and compared with that of a standard MPC, showing good improvement.
item.dc:creator: Danilo Saccani, Lorenzo Fagiano

item.title: EgoDepth-Bench: Benchmarking Metric Depth for Egocentric Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce EgoDepth-Bench, comprising 941,233 synchronized samples collected across 37 distinct physical environments. Each sample combines six calibrated RGB views with metric depth in the native fisheye view, reconstructed from five active-infrared stereo modules. A calibrated ball-bar confirms millimeter-level geometric accuracy, with a median error of 1.27 mm on a known sphere spacing. Environment-held-out splits enable evaluation of generalization to unseen environments. Across monocular, stereo, and multi-view models, the benchmark measures both depth accuracy and prediction coverage, including on hands and objects. Fine-tuning MapAnything on EgoDepth-Bench reduces metric AbsRel from 0.708 to 0.091 and scale-aligned AbsRel from 0.327 to 0.072 on unseen environments. These results demonstrate that EgoDepth-Bench provides effective supervision and enables rigorous evaluation of metric and relative depth estimation in egocentric manipulation. The project page provides the evaluation code and interactive RGB-depth sequences.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Gao, Dongchen Wei, Xinyang Lin, Shuhua Cao, Xueliang Guo, Zhuohan Li, Yihao Wang

item.title: Can Multimodal Fusion MakeSense for Embodied Vision in Degraded Sensing?
item.description: arXiv:2611.30836v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.
item.dc:creator: Cheng-Ru Chou, Shih-Yu Lai, Pei-Lin Chiang, Shou-Po Tsai, Jing-Zhe Huang, Fukuharu Tanaka, Hirozumi Yamaguchi, Bing-Yu Chen, Yu-Lun Liu, Hsun-Ping Hsieh

item.title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.30898v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
item.dc:creator: Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy

item.title: GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind
item.description: arXiv:2611.30900v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.
item.dc:creator: Anh Dao, Quan-Dung Pham, Danh Vinh Le, Tuyen Pham Le, Quan Nguyen, Yuzhang Shang

item.title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
item.description: arXiv:2611.31240v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.
item.dc:creator: Seongchan Kim, Soowon Son, Sangoh Kim, Hyunah Ko, Eunbeen Hong, Hyunkoo Lee, Sanghyun Lee, WonJun Moon, Kihong Kim, Dongyeon Son, Woongchan Nam, Seungryong Kim

item.title: PRIMA: Preference-Informed Multimodal Trajectory Planning with Vision-Language Model for Autonomous Driving
item.description: arXiv:2412.04209v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decision-making and motion planning constitute critical components for ensuring the safety and efficiency of autonomous vehicles (AVs). Existing methodologies typically adopt two paradigms: decision then planning or generation then scoring. However, the former architecture often suffers from decision-planning misalignment that incurs risky situations. Meanwhile, the latter struggles to balance short-term operational metrics (e.g., immediate motion smoothness) with long-term tactical goals (e.g., route efficiency), resulting in myopic or overly conservative behaviors. To address these issues, we introduce PRIMA, a preference-informed multimodal trajectory planning framework assisted by a Vision-Language Model (VLM). Our approach employs a tri-stage cognitive decomposition protocol, encompassing scene understanding, action selection, and confidence assessment, to generate diverse candidate actions paired with verbalized confidence scores. This reasoning mechanism exposes alternative tactical choices and provides an empirical preference signal for balancing them with downstream planning quality. Furthermore, we propose a novel planning module that integrates a diffusion model for trajectory generation and a hierarchical refinement process to find the optimal trajectory. This enables the selection over trajectory candidates accounting for both low-level solution quality and high-level tactical preferences, avoiding the risks within one-shot decisions and overcoming the limitations of short-sighted scoring mechanisms. Comprehensive simulation-based closed-loop evaluations on nuPlan and InterPlan demonstrate competitive performance across common and long-tail benchmarks. A paired controlled intervention further evaluates the incremental decision utility of the verbalized confidence signal. The code will be released upon acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Ruoyu Yao, Yubin Wang, Haichao Liu, Rui Yang, Zengqi Peng, Lei Zhu, Jun Ma

item.title: Fitts' List Revisited: An Empirical Study on Function Allocation in a Two-Agent Physical Human-Robot Collaborative Position/Force Task
item.description: arXiv:2505.04722v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this letter, we investigate whether classical function allocation-the principle of assigning tasks to either a human or a machine-holds for physical Human-Robot Collaboration, which is important for providing insights for Industry 5.0 to guide how to best augment rather than replace workers. This study empirically tests the applicability of Fitts' List within physical Human-Robot Collaboration, by conducting a user study (N=26, within-subject design) to evaluate four distinct allocations of position/force control between human and robot in an abstract blending task. We hypothesize that the function in which humans control the position achieves better performance and receives higher user ratings. When allocating position control to the human and force control to the robot, compared to the opposite case, we observed a significant improvement in preventing overblending. This was also perceived better in terms of physical demand and overall system acceptance, while participants experienced greater autonomy, more engagement and less frustration. An interesting insight was that the supervisory role (when the robot controls both position and force) was rated second best in terms of subjective acceptance. Another surprising insight was that if position control was delegated to the robot, the participants perceived much lower autonomy than when the force control was delegated to the robot. These findings empirically support applying Fitts' principles to static function allocation for physical collaboration, while also revealing important nuanced user experience trade-offs, particularly regarding perceived autonomy when delegating position control.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, Volume 11, Issue 1, January 2026
item.dc:creator: Nicky Mol, J. Micah Prendergast, David A. Abbink, Luka Peternel

item.title: DUViN: Diffusion-Based Underwater Visual Navigation via Knowledge-Transferred Depth Features
item.description: arXiv:2509.02983v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous underwater navigation remains a challenging problem due to limited sensing capabilities and the difficulty of constructing accurate maps in underwater environments. In this paper, we propose a Diffusion-based Underwater Visual Navigation policy via knowledge-transferred depth features, named DUViN, which enables vision-based end-to-end 4-DoF motion control for underwater vehicles in unknown environments. DUViN guides the vehicle to avoid obstacles and maintain a safe and perception-aware altitude relative to the terrain without relying on pre-built maps. To address the difficulty of collecting large-scale underwater navigation datasets, we propose a method that enables transfer under domain shifts from simulation with clear images to underwater environments by leveraging depth features and introducing a novel model transfer strategy. Specifically, our training framework consists of two phases: we first train the diffusion-based visual navigation policy on a clear image dataset collected in simulation using a pre-trained depth feature extractor. Secondly, we retrain the extractor on an underwater depth estimation task and integrate the adapted extractor into the trained navigation policy from the first phase. Experiments conducted in simulation and in an indoor water tank provide proof-of-concept validation of the effectiveness and sim-to-real transferability of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Jinghe Yang, Minh-Quan Le, Mingming Gong, Ye Pu

item.title: Neural 3D Object Reconstruction with Small-Scale Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
item.description: arXiv:2509.12458v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Miniaturized Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) can access indoor and hard-to-reach spaces, but severe constraints on payload and autonomy have limited their use in demanding tasks such as high-quality 3D reconstruction. We introduce a novel system architecture that enables autonomous, high-fidelity 3D scanning of static objects with sub-100 gram UAVs. Our core innovation lies in a closed-loop active viewpoint selection framework specifically tailored for ultra-constrained micro-platforms, advancing beyond standard static or offline active reconstruction methods. The framework establishes a dual-reconstruction pipeline that creates a real-time (RT) feedback loop between data capture and flight control. A near-RT process uses Structure-from-Motion (SfM) to generate an instantaneous point-cloud of the object. A systematic trajectory adaptation algorithm analyzes the model quality on the fly and dynamically adapts the UAV's trajectory based on parameterized spatial partitioning to intelligently capture new images of poorly covered areas, ensuring comprehensive acquisition. For the final, high-fidelity output, a non-RT pipeline employs a Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)-based Neural 3D Reconstruction (N3DR) approach, fusing SfM-derived camera poses with precise external location data, evaluated across both radio-based Ultra Wideband (UWB) and visual motion-capture setups, to correct sensor noise and achieve superior accuracy. We implemented and validated this architecture using Crazyflie 2.1 UAVs. Our experiments, conducted in both single- and multi-UAV configurations show that algorithmic dynamic trajectory adaptation consistently improves reconstruction quality over static flight paths. This work demonstrates a scalable and autonomous solution that unlocks the potential of miniaturized UAVs for fine-grained 3D reconstruction, a capability previously reserved for much larger platforms.
item.dc:creator: \`Almos Veres-Vit\`alyos, Filip Lemic, Daniel Johannes Bugelnig, Joan Bernaus Casades\'us, Genis Castillo Gomez-Raya, Sergi Abadal, Bernhard Rinner, Xavier Costa-P\'erez

item.title: Teleoperator-Aware and CBF-Based Adaptive Nonlinear MPC for Shared Autonomy in Obstacle Avoidance of Legged Robots
item.description: arXiv:2509.22815v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safe and effective collaboration between humans and autonomous legged robots is a fundamental challenge in shared autonomy, particularly for teleoperated systems navigating cluttered environments. Shared autonomy for legged robots remains challenging due to uncertain human commands, collision-avoidance requirements, and the need to coordinate high-level planning with dynamically feasible locomotion. This paper presents a teleoperator-aware, control barrier function (CBF)-based, adaptive nonlinear model predictive control (ANMPC) framework for shared autonomy of quadrupedal robots in obstacle-avoidance tasks. The framework employs a prescribed arbitration weight between human and robot actions while modeling human inputs using a noisily rational Boltzmann model, whose parameters are adapted online through a projected gradient descent (PGD) law based on observed joystick commands. CBF constraints are incorporated into a computationally efficient NMPC formulation to promote obstacle avoidance while accounting for predicted human actions. The hierarchical architecture integrates high-level CBF-based ANMPC (10 Hz), mid-level dynamics-aware NMPC (60 Hz) enforcing single rigid body (SRB) dynamics, and low-level nonlinear whole-body control (500 Hz). Human-in-the-loop hardware experiments with ten participants on a Unitree Go2 quadruped demonstrate real-time feasibility and collision-free navigation across 50 trials. Shared autonomy reduced average human control effort by 51% and joystick activity from 88% to 42% of trial time, with comparable obstacle clearance and significantly higher perceived assistance than manual operation. Simulation-based ablation studies demonstrate improved obstacle clearance across operator rationality levels and up to a 66% reduction in median human-action prediction error through online adaptation.
item.dc:creator: Ruturaj Sambhus, Muneeb Ahmad, Basit Muhammad Imran, Sujith Vijayan, Dylan P. Losey, Kaveh Akbari Hamed

item.title: Injecting Hallucinations in Autonomous Vehicles: A Component-Agnostic Safety Evaluation Framework
item.description: arXiv:2510.07749v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Perception failures in autonomous vehicles (AV) remain a major safety concern because they can directly compromise decision-making and contribute to unsafe behavior. To study how these failures affect safety, researchers typically inject artificial faults into real-world or simulated components and observe the resulting outcomes. However, existing fault injection (FI) studies often target a single sensor within the machine perception (MP) module, resulting in siloed frameworks that are difficult to generalize or integrate into unified simulation environments. This work addresses that limitation by reframing perception failures as hallucinations, that is, false perceptions that distort an AV's situational awareness and may trigger unsafe control actions. Building on this concept, we propose a configurable, component-agnostic hallucination injection framework that induces six plausible hallucination types in an open-source simulation environment. A total of 18,356 simulations (8,695 baseline and 9,661 with hallucinations injected) were executed while AVs crossed an unsignalized intersection with transversal traffic. The results statistically validate the framework and quantify the impact of each hallucination type on collisions and on the minimum distance between the AV and the nearest vehicle, used as a continuous proxy for the safety margin. Certain hallucinations, especially missed detection, blind region, angular drift, phantom perception, and latency, significantly increase the odds of collision, while linear drift significantly reduces minimum distances without producing a statistically significant increase in collision odds in the evaluated scenario. The proposed framework provides a scalable and statistically grounded method for evaluating AV safety under perception distortions and supports future research on fault tolerance and resilient AV design.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Moreira Nascimento, Gabriel Kenji Godoy Shimanuki, L\'ucio Flavio Vismari, Jo\~ao Batista Camargo Jr, Jorge Rady de Almeida Jr, Paulo Sergio Cugnasca, Anna Carolina Muller Queiroz, Jeremy Noah Bailenson

item.title: Orientation Learning and Adaptation towards Simultaneous Incorporation of Multiple Local Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2510.07986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Orientation learning plays a pivotal role in many tasks. However, the rotation group SO(3) is a Riemannian manifold. As a result, the distortion caused by non-Euclidean geometric nature introduces difficulties to the incorporation of local constraints, especially for the simultaneous incorporation of multiple local constraints. To address this issue, we propose the Angle-Axis Space-based orientation representation method to solve several orientation learning problems, including orientation adaptation and minimization of angular acceleration. Specifically, we propose a weighted average mechanism in SO(3) based on the angle-axis representation method. Our main idea is to generate multiple trajectories by considering different local constraints at different basepoints. Then these multiple trajectories are fused to generate a smooth trajectory by our proposed weighted average mechanism, achieving the goal to incorporate multiple local constraints simultaneously. Compared with existing solution, ours can address the distortion issue and make the off-theshelf Euclidean learning algorithm be re-applicable in non-Euclidean space. Simulation and Experimental evaluations validate that our solution can not only adapt orientations towards arbitrary desired via-points and cope with angular acceleration constraints, but also incorporate multiple local constraints simultaneously to achieve extra benefits, e.g., achieving smaller acceleration costs.
item.dc:creator: Gaofeng Li, Peisen Xu, Ruize Wang, Qi Ye, Dezhen Song, Jiming Chen, Yanlong Huang

item.title: A Shared-Autonomy Construction Robotic System for Overhead Works
item.description: arXiv:2511.09695v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the ongoing development of a robotic system for overhead work such as ceiling drilling. The hardware platform comprises a mobile base with a two-stage lift, on which a bimanual torso is mounted with a custom-designed drilling end effector and RGB-D cameras. To support teleoperation in dynamic environments with limited visibility, we use Gaussian splatting for online 3D reconstruction and introduce motion parameters to model moving objects. For safe operation around dynamic obstacles, we developed a neural configuration-space barrier approach for planning and control. Initial feasibility studies demonstrate the capability of the hardware in drilling, bolting, and anchoring, and the software in safe teleoperation in a dynamic environment. Experiment videos and results are available at https://kmk9846.github.io/Construction-Robot/
item.dc:creator: David Minkwan Kim, K. M. Brian Lee, Yong Hyeok Seo, Nikola Raicevic, Runfa Blark Li, Kehan Long, Chan Seon Yoon, Dong Min Kang, Byeong Jo Lim, Young Pyoung Kim, Nikolay Atanasov, Truong Nguyen, Se Woong Jun, Young Ouk Kim

item.title: Latent Reasoning VLA: Latent Thinking and Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.01166v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models benefit from chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but existing approaches incur high inference overhead and rely on discrete reasoning representations that mismatch continuous perception and control. We propose Latent Reasoning VLA (LaRA-VLA), a unified VLA framework that internalizes multi-modal CoT reasoning into continuous latent representations for embodied action. LaRA-VLA performs unified reasoning and prediction in latent space, eliminating explicit CoT generation at inference time and enabling efficient, action-oriented control. To realize latent embodied reasoning, we introduce a curriculum-based training paradigm that progressively transitions from explicit textual and visual CoT supervision to latent reasoning, and finally adapts latent reasoning dynamics to condition action generation. We construct two structured CoT datasets and evaluate LaRA-VLA on both simulation benchmarks and long-horizon real-robot manipulation tasks. Experimental results show that LaRA-VLA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art VLA methods while reducing inference latency by up to 90\% compared to explicit CoT-based approaches, demonstrating latent reasoning as an effective and efficient paradigm for real-time embodied control. Project Page: https://loveju1y.github.io/Latent-Reasoning-VLA/
item.dc:creator: Shuanghao Bai, Jing Lyu, Wanqi Zhou, Zhe Li, Dakai Wang, Lei Xing, Xiaoguang Zhao, Pengwei Wang, Zhongyuan Wang, Cheng Chi, Badong Chen, Shanghang Zhang

item.title: UNILARN: Latent Action Pretraining with Dedicated RGB, Depth, and Unified RGB-Depth Supervision
item.description: arXiv:2602.20231v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Depth provides critical geometric supervision for robot manipulation, yet existing depth-aware policies typically inject it through fused representations or auxiliary objectives, leaving its role in action learning implicit. We introduce UNILARN, a latent-action pretraining framework that explicitly preserves three complementary supervisory targets from RGB-D transitions: RGB-specific, depth-specific, and unified latent actions. RGB and depth transition embeddings are first discretized through a shared codebook, then fused and re-quantized through a separate unified codebook, preserving modality-specific dynamics while modeling their shared action semantics. These three latent-action targets provide separate pseudo-action supervision during VLA pretraining, avoiding both inconsistent independent learning and premature multimodal fusion without requiring robot action labels. The pretrained VLA is subsequently fine-tuned on executable actions and requires only RGB observations and language instructions at inference. Experiments in simulation and the real-world show improvements over RGB-based latent-action pretraining, particularly on geometry-sensitive manipulation tasks.
item.dc:creator: Manish Kumar Govind, Dominick Reilly, Pu Wang, Hieu Le, Srijan Das

item.title: SG-DOR: Learning Scene Graphs with Direction-Conditioned Occlusion Reasoning for Pepper Plants
item.description: arXiv:2603.06512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robotic harvesting in dense crop canopies requires effective interventions that depend not only on geometry, but also on explicit, direction-conditioned relations identifying which organs obstruct a target fruit. We present SG-DOR (Scene Graphs with Direction-Conditioned Occlusion Reasoning), a relational framework that, given instance-segmented organ point clouds, infers a scene graph encoding physical attachments and direction-conditioned occlusion. We introduce an \emph{occlusion ranking} task for retrieving and ranking candidate leaves for a target fruit and approach direction, and propose a direction-aware graph neural architecture with per-fruit leaf-set attention and union-level aggregation. Experiments on a multi-plant synthetic pepper dataset show improved occlusion prediction (F1=0.73, NDCG@3=0.85) and attachment inference (edge F1=0.83) over strong ablations, yielding a structured relational signal for downstream intervention planning.
item.dc:creator: Rohit Menon, Niklas Mueller-Goldingen, Sicong Pan, Gokul Krishna Chenchani, Maren Bennewitz

item.title: Perception-Aware Multi-UAV Implicit Coordination in the Wild
item.description: arXiv:2603.08379v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a perception-aware 3D navigation system for decentralized multi-robot coordination in cluttered environments, such as forests with dense canopy cover where GNSS is unavailable. Our novel perception-aware approach computes collision-free motion toward a goal region while accounting for the limited field of view of the sensor, and is combined with a replanner to guide multiple robots to their goal. The system relies on an onboard anisotropic 3D LiDAR, used for localization, mapping, and detection of obstacles and neighboring robots. Decentralized coordination among the robots emerges as a byproduct of local interactions and common rules, so no explicit communication is required. The system is evaluated through extensive single and multi-robot simulations across diverse scenarios and validated in multiple real-world field experiments.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Boldrer, Michal Kamler, Afzal Ahmad, Martin Saska

item.title: RankFormer: A Propose-then-Select Transformer for Multi-Agent Multimodal Trajectory Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2604.07126v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting traffic agent trajectories plays an important role in autonomous driving, traffic operations, transportation safety analysis, etc. Although many deep learning algorithms are devised to predict future agent trajectories, the trajectory prediction problem is still challenging due to the complexity of decision-making process, interactions with surrounding vehicles, and the existence of multiple possible intentions for the traveling agents even under similar scenarios. Most existing methods are limited by the requirement of graph structures (e.g., Graph Neural Network) or the requirement of manually labeled intentions. In this study, we propose a pure Transformer-based deep learning model for multi-modal trajectory prediction considering temporal dependencies and agent-agent spatial interactions. After encoding the historical trajectories, two parallel decoders are employed to generate trajectories and probabilities on separate decoder tracks. The model is evaluated on two real-world datasets, one highway dataset and the other pedestrian dataset with solid performance. One important insight is that following a ``propose-then-select'' strategy, the agent-agent spatial interactions are only considered for probability estimation instead of trajectory generation. In summary, the proposed model provides a potential direction to design more robust and effective multi-modal trajectory prediction models.
item.dc:creator: Diyi Liu, Zihan Niu, Tu Xu, Xingchen Zhang, Lishan Sun

item.title: FreqCache: Frequency-Enhanced Token Caching for Efficient Streaming VLN Models
item.description: arXiv:2604.24391v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Streaming vision-and-language navigation (VLN) repeatedly encodes overlapping views. Robot motion can shift a reusable patch to a different position, while small residual shifts near an edge can change its feature. These effects complicate both patch selection and the choice of a reuse budget for each frame. We present FreqCache, a streaming VLN caching framework that integrates frequency-domain characteristics from raw observations with token-level redundancy identification. We analyze their complementarity in cross-frame correspondence, reuse validity, and cache budgeting. Our analysis shows that spectral magnitude and phase cues can recover spatially shifted correspondences, local high-frequency characteristics can reveal structurally sensitive tokens, and single-frame spectral entropy can guide the budget among eligible patches. Based on these insights, FreqCache introduces frequency-enhanced token alignment, selective token refresh, and adaptive cache budgeting to reduce redundant computation while preserving navigation performance. On R2R-CE, FreqCache cuts per-step latency by 6.7--12.0\% relative to VLN-Cache and speeds up inference by up to $1.64\times$ over the original models. Across R2R-CE and RxR-CE, success rate drops by at most 0.7 percentage points.
item.dc:creator: Zihao Zheng, Hangyu Cao, Qichao Ma, Xichang Wu, Zhihao Mao, Lingyue Zhang, Maoliang Li, Jiayu Chen, Donggang Cao, Xuanzhe Liu, Hong Mei, Xiang Chen

item.title: Self-Supervised Online Robot-Agnostic Traversability Estimation for Open-World Environments
item.description: arXiv:2605.28442v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised online traversability estimation enables robots to continuously learn from unlabeled open-world experiences and adapt their navigation behavior toward safe and efficient trajectories. Existing approaches either rely on handcrafted proprioceptive traversability scores, limiting robot-agnosticism, or cluster prior data, preventing online learning. Moreover, many continual learning methods incur substantial memory and computational costs, hindering onboard deployment. We introduce COTRATE, an online learning framework for continuous traversability estimation from multimodal, unlabeled robot experience. Our method first infers robust traversability scores using a robot-agnostic, learning-based online terrain assessment module operating on proprioceptiveand inertial signals. These scores then supervise a visual traversability network through a novel alignment loss that associates visual embeddings with online terrain assessments. To mitigate forgetting during continual learning with minimal overhead, we propose a diversity-aware feature selection strategythat preserves performance using a compact replay memory. We further show that the learned traversability representation supports knowledge transfer across different robot platforms with different locomotion kinematics. We evaluate COTRATE on a dataset of $\approx$ 50,000 images collected with two robotic platforms across 11 outdoor terrains, and benchmark it on navigation tasks in three representative outdoor environments. We make the dataset, code, and trained models publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Julia Hindel, Simon Bultmann, Houman Masnavi, Daniele Cattaneo, Abhinav Valada

item.title: 3DVLA: Enhancing Vision-Language-Action Models via 3D Spatial and Instance Understanding
item.description: arXiv:2605.29416v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, yet they suffer from a critical limitation: a lack of 3D scene understanding. This deficiency manifests as three intertwined challenges: weak extraction of 3D spatial positions without enforcing multi-view consistency, inadequate 3D instance understanding, and fragile reasoning under occlusion. Although mature 3D perception methods exist, their direct integration into VLA pipelines is hindered by architectural incompatibility and by heavy reliance on costly instance-level annotations. To address these challenges, we propose 3DVLA, a framework compatible with existing VLA models, which introduces 3D understanding without requiring extra manual labels or discarding VLM priors. Specifically, 3DVLA tackles the three challenges through: (1) pervasive 3D feature encoding with explicit multi-view consistency constraints across all modalities and a Spatially-Conditioned Geometry Aggregation method, (2) an object-centric 3D instance module with high-level instance tokens for 3D instance awareness, and (3) a masked self-supervised 3D encoding branch that retains its predictor for visual token completion to handle occlusions. We integrate 3DVLA with multiple VLA baselines and evaluate on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world settings. Results show consistent and significant gains in manipulation performance, validating both the effectiveness and plug-and-play compatibility of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyu Xia, Yousen Tang, Bingqing Wei, Yongtao Wang

item.title: DriveAnchor: Progressive Anchor-based Flow Learning for Autonomous Driving Planning
item.description: arXiv:2606.00519v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous-driving planners must generate route- and maneuver-compliant trajectories under a limited decoder-call budget while adapting offline to black-box static-collision feedback. We propose DriveAnchor, a three-stage framework built around a shared vocabulary of recorded trajectories and a continuous trajectory interface. The vocabulary supports flow-matching (FM) residual learning, Energy Field (EF) corridor-conditioned initialization, and anchor-guided zeroth-order reward fine-tuning. The reward update operates in trajectory space without policy likelihoods or reward gradients, enabling offline adaptation of a deterministic decoder. On sampled nuPlan scenarios, EF guidance and reward fine-tuning each improve the mean closed-loop score. On the same cases, the official pretrained Diffusion Planner scores higher with our reward update than with supervised fine-tuning. We further integrate the trajectory generator into a real vehicle's planning pipeline and demonstrate its operation on urban roads. On 10,000 held-out internal scenarios, under the original non-EF prior and a fixed two-call FM budget, reward fine-tuning reduces short- and long-horizon static candidate collision rates from 27.22% and 56.54% to 2.94% and 7.15%, respectively, and improves 8-s best-of-set minADE from 2.27 to 1.34 m. In a separate junction diagnostic on checkpoints before Stage 3, one and two EF calls raise corridor-guidance satisfaction from 22.10% to 74.13% and 87.92%, respectively. Additional ablations support the vocabulary size and the anchor-guided sampling configuration. On NVIDIA Drive Orin, two EF calls and two FM calls take 2.06 ms per scene on average. Code and deployment videos are available on the project page: https://driveanchor-meituan.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Limin Yan, Haoyun Tang, Yutao Qiu, Hongqing Liu, Zhandong Mei, Haoyu Xu

item.title: Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filtering for Data-Efficient Joint Tracking and Classification
item.description: arXiv:2606.02767v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kalman filtering performance is highly sensitive to model mismatch and noise covariance tuning. Classical adaptive filtering methods address these issues by estimating model parameters or noise covariances from measurement data but rely on a predefined model structure. Learning-based methods provide greater flexibility but typically require large supervised datasets and often lack well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. This article proposes a self-supervised Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter (HAKF) that learns time-varying corrections to the system dynamics and process-noise covariance directly from measurements while jointly estimating the measurement-noise covariance. Because these corrections are learned from measurements alone, we analyze the structural identifiability of the corresponding time-invariant parameterizations. For a constant-velocity model with position-only measurements, an unrestricted process-noise covariance is not identifiable even when the dynamics are known, whereas a physically structured parameterization that couples the dynamics and process covariance is jointly identifiable with the measurement-noise covariance. This analysis motivates a structured HAKF variant, compared with a flexible variant that adapts the dynamics and process covariance independently. The innovation likelihood of HAKF also enables model classification through generalized Bayesian inference. In Isaac Lab simulations, the structured HAKF improves tracking accuracy over a fitted Kalman filter across all training-set sizes. When training data are limited, its advantage over the flexible variant is largest, and it outperforms a supervised recurrent neural network in both tracking and classification. On recorded DPJAIT flight trajectories, it achieves the best tracking and classification performance with near-consistent state covariance, whereas the flexible variant becomes overconfident.
item.dc:creator: Jiho Lee, Nisar R. Ahmed, Rebecca Russell

item.title: OASIS: From Simulation Data Collection to Real-World Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2606.08548v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent progress in robot manipulation has been largely driven by learning from large-scale demonstrations. For humanoid robot loco-manipulation tasks, however, existing data sources force an unsatisfying tradeoff between trajectory quality and scalability. Real-world teleoperation provides the highest-quality trajectories but requires dedicated physical space and time-consuming scene resets. Simulation offers an alternative way out of this dilemma: it can produce clean, embodiment-aligned data at scale without any physical hardware. In this paper, we propose OASIS, a simulation-data-driven framework for humanoid loco-manipulation. OASIS automatically reconstructs realistic object assets from real-world images using a 3D generative model. Based on these assets, trajectories are first collected through teleoperation in simulation, and then augmented under diverse domain randomizations in a post-processing stage. With the resulting simulation data, we further design a hierarchical visuomotor policy for humanoid loco-manipulation. Extensive experiments on the real humanoid robot show that, under zero-shot deployment, the policy trained on our simulation data achieves higher success rates on most tasks than that trained on real-robot teleoperation data, owing largely to the broad lighting and environmental variations covered by our simulation rendering, which real-robot data fails to capture. The project page is available at https://oasis-humanoid.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Zehao Yu, Jiakun Zheng, Weiji Xie, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li

item.title: YUBI: Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation at Scale
item.description: arXiv:2606.10244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Yielding Universal Bidigital Interface (YUBI), a finger-aligned gripper designed to enable intuitive, ergonomic, and scalable data collection for bimanual dexterous manipulation. While handheld data collection systems such as Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) enable affordable data collection, their bulky pistol-grip designs can pose ergonomic and usability challenges for fine-grained, dexterous manipulation tasks. To address this, YUBI presents a distinct design principle: yielding, finger-driven actuation that directly maps human finger movements to gripper jaw motion. Using the YUBI devices, we set up a data collection system with integrated VR-based 6 DoF tracking of the gripper, ensuring high-fidelity trajectory data acquisition. We curate a UMI-based dataset of unprecedented scale: 8,434 hours across 1.20M episodes and 119 tasks. Experiments show that YUBI offers advantages over the UMI gripper in versatility for complex bimanual tasks, dexterity, and operational efficiency. A single policy trained on the YUBI dataset transfers across multiple bimanual robots (UR, Franka, and ELEY) simply by mounting the gripper on each platform, confirming that the collected data are directly executable as policy supervision. We release the gripper hardware, data-collection software, and dataset as one integrated stack, offering the open community a reproducible path to large-scale data acquisition for advancing robotic foundation models.
item.dc:creator: Takehiko Ohkawa, Jumpei Arima, Yuki Noguchi, Masatoshi Tateno, Makoto Sugiura, Takuya Okubo, Kengo Ikeuchi, Yuma Shin, Hiroki Nishizawa, Naoaki Kanazawa, Yuki Wakayama, Daiki Fukunaga, Koshi Makihara, Tomohiro Motoda, Floris Erich, Yukiyasu Domae, Tatsuya Matsushima, Yohishiro Okumatsu, Kei Ota

item.title: Stubborn: A Streamlined and Unified Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robust Motion Tracking and Fall Recovery for Humanoids
item.description: arXiv:2606.12814v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent reinforcement learning approaches have shown great promise in improving humanoid motion tracking performance and achieving fall recovery under disturbances. However, most existing works treat motion tracking and fall recovery as different tasks and require multi-stage training with specialized recovery rewards and/or separate recovery policies. Moreover, existing reinforcement learning-based methods often terminate training episodes immediately after severe tracking failures, limiting recovery-oriented exploration in unstable or fallen states. To address the above issues, we propose Stubborn, a streamlined and unified reinforcement learning framework to achieve robust humanoid motion tracking and fall recovery. Specifically, Stubborn uses an asymmetric Actor-Critic architecture and consists of three major components. First, a yaw-aligned tracking representation is adopted to reduce sensitivity to global drift and heading disturbances while preserving gravity-related balance information. Second, we introduce a Bernoulli-based probabilistic termination mechanism that enables the policy to encourage exploration of fall-recovery behaviors under varying failure modes. Third, we propose a probabilistic termination and tracking-error-driven strategy that dynamically reshapes the sampling distribution based on tracking performance, increasing the training efficiency for difficult motion segments and unstable states. Extensive comparisons with SOTA methods and ablation studies show that Stubborn achieved competitive performance and avoided the reward-hacking tendency of baseline methods, and the proposed probabilistic termination mechanism and adaptive sampling strategy contributed to the performance and robustness gains. For real-world demonstrations, please refer to the project page at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/Stubborn/.
item.dc:creator: Yuhui Yang, Xiao Ren, Zongbiao Weng, Zhijie Liu, He Kong

item.title: $\lambda$-Reachability: Geometric-Horizon Safety Bellman Equations for Humanoid Safety
item.description: arXiv:2606.16022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce $\lambda$-Reachability, a scalable approach to Hamilton--Jacobi safety analysis for high-dimensional robotic systems. Unlike prior discounted formulations that rely on fixed one-step Bellman updates, $\lambda$-Reachability employs a stochastic multi-step estimator of the safety value, using a geometrically distributed rollout horizon together with a randomly absorbed terminal. Conceptually analogous to TD($\lambda$), $\lambda$-Reachability interpolates between local self-consistency updates and long-horizon max-over-trajectory safety targets via an interpretable horizon-control parameter. Unlike TD($\lambda$), where the terminal value is always incorporated in learning targets, the terminal safety value in $\lambda$-Reachability is only used at a probability controlled by parameter $\delta$. We formally show that for $\delta<1$, the update induces a contraction mapping that allows temporal-difference learning; as $\lambda \to 1$, the estimator recovers the undiscounted reachability objective. We apply $\lambda$-Reachability to high-dimensional safety learning problems with both simulated and real humanoid robots under balance and collision avoidance constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that $\lambda$-Reachability significantly improves both safe-set boundary classification and safety margin estimation compared to single-step temporal-difference baselines.
item.dc:creator: Rui Chen, Shangtao Li, Yifan Sun, Changliu Liu

item.title: Learning from Failure: Robot Self-Improvement via Human Videos
item.description: arXiv:2606.21406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning from deployment experience is essential for robots to improve their performance in the real world. A robot should be able to learn from failed executions, but these do not reveal which actions would have succeeded, and obtaining corrections from human experts requires costly monitoring and intervention. Human videos offer a rich source of interaction experience, showing how actions change the environment and lead to task completion. To turn this experience into corrective supervision, we introduce Dynamics-Guided Action Correction (DGAC), which uses dynamics and value models pretrained on human videos to construct alternative actions at failed states and evaluate their outcomes without executing each candidate. We evaluate our method on seven real-world manipulation tasks across two robot embodiments and demonstrate that it improves the average success rate from 40% to 81%, requiring no expert corrections during self-improvement. We further show that generated corrections enable recovery from failed executions and provide more effective training targets than imagined policy rollouts using the same models and data. Finally, we demonstrate that human-video dynamics and value models provide effective corrective supervision for policies pretrained on either human or robot data, suggesting that human videos benefit robot learning in addition to policy initialization.
item.dc:creator: Hanzhi Chen, Anran Zhang, Simon Schaefer, Kejia Chen, Shi Chen, Daniel Cremers, Oier Mees, Stefan Leutenegger

item.title: PAC-ACT: Post-training Actor-Critic for Action Chunking Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2607.09590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Precision industrial contact manipulation requires reliable robot policies under pose perturbations and contact-force constraints. Vision-language-action models offer broad generalization but often introduce high inference latency and GPU-memory cost, while vision-action chunking policies are more suitable for real-time industrial control. However, these policies are usually trained by behavior cloning and suffer from distribution shift in contact-rich tasks. This paper proposes PAC-ACT, a reinforcement-learning post-training framework for pretrained Action Chunking Transformer policies. PAC-ACT reformulates policy optimization at the chunk level, constructs an ACT-transferred actor-critic architecture, and introduces a hybrid behavior-prior constraint to preserve the pretrained action distribution during online fine-tuning. Experiments on industrial precision-contact benchmarks show that PAC-ACT improves task success, contact stability, and force safety while retaining low latency and low GPU-memory usage. On the Contour task, PAC-ACT significantly reduces peak contact force and decreases the proportion of force readings above 60 N by 46 times. Sparse-reward ablations further show that the proposed behavior-prior constraint enables effective exploration under randomized initial poses.
item.dc:creator: Yujie Pang, Zudong Li, Leran Chen, Yongsheng Ma

item.title: Video2Track: Steerable Adversarial Scenario Generation from Real-World Interaction Videos to Proving Grounds for Automated Driving System Testing
item.description: arXiv:2608.11592v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physical proving-ground testing enables controlled and repeatable validation of automated driving systems (ADSs). However, existing approaches often rely on manually designed reference routes and scripted vehicle behaviors, limiting deployment efficiency, real-world interaction reproduction, and interaction risk steerability. To address these limitations, we propose Video2Track, a framework that converts real-world driving videos into steerable adversarial scenarios for proving-ground testing. Video2Track extracts interaction semantics using a vision-language model, retrieves compatible maneuver pairs on the target road network, and generates reference trajectories through interaction-guided diffusion. Game-based online refinement adjusts background vehicle (BV) trajectories based on real-time feedback from the vehicle under test (VUT) to regulate interaction risk toward a prescribed anticipated post-encroachment time (APET). Video2Track achieved an interaction consistency rate of 82.1\% and a scenario generation success rate of 78.6\%. In proving-ground tests, the mean minimum APET was within 0.5~s of each of the four target values. Video2Track also achieved lower mean minimum APET values than the evaluated baselines in both cut-in and unprotected left-turn scenarios. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring real-world driving interactions to executable proving-ground scenarios, enabling faithful interaction reproduction and steerable adversarial testing on an Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled 5G cloud-controlled platform.
item.dc:creator: Mengjie Tian, Xinrui Zhang, Tianyu Li, Peizhi Zhang, Guirong Zhuo, Haojie Feng, Ziyi Yin, Qixiang Zhang, Lu Xiong

item.title: WM-VS: Progress-Aligned World Models for Closed-Loop Visual Servoing
item.description: arXiv:2609.20892v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Closed-loop visual servoing requires predictions that indicate whether an action reduces task error, not only whether the action is plausible. We call this gap the prediction-control mismatch and introduce WM-VS, a target-centric progress-aligned world-model framework for closed-loop visual servoing. Offline target-region DINOv2 correspondences define a signed four-dimensional servo coordinate for translation, scale, and in-plane rotation. Stage 1 aligns action-conditioned latent transitions with this coordinate; Stage 2 freezes the world model and trains a reactive joint-velocity policy with action imitation, consequence supervision, and short imagined rollouts that favor error contraction. Deployment is RGB-only and reactive, without online trajectory optimization. On a real 7-DoF eye-to-hand system, WM-VS reaches a corner RMSE no larger than 10 percent of its initial value in 30/30 trials and retains this criterion at the final valid frame in 25/30 (83.33 percent). Removing future-error alignment reduces retention to 26.67 percent. The learned progress signal agrees with an external AprilTag corner error not used for training or control (mean Spearman rho = 0.8778). Without retraining, two unseen 3D targets achieve translation-error reductions of 86.48 percent and 90.27 percent and rotation-error reductions of 70.01 percent and 65.70 percent. These results link progress-aligned action consequences to repeated closed-loop correction and transfer. Code and data will be released as open source.
item.dc:creator: Guanzhong Sun, Junyi Ma, Yixuan Zhou, Yuxuan Wu, Yanzi Miao, Hesheng Wang

item.title: CHOREO: From Single Skill to Continuous Humanoid Execution
item.description: arXiv:2609.22274v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Motion data, RL policies, and generative models give humanoids thousands of skills, and the best general trackers execute nearly all of them alone. Chained to follow a language instruction, the skills fail far more often: in simulation, even the best of eight trackers reaches only 84.9\% sequence success, and their average is 48.9\%. This is because validating a skill alone certifies it only for the tracker that ran it and the state it started from, whereas a sequence keeps one tracker and starts each skill wherever the last one ended. Prior work meets these two conditions mostly by training; CHOREO restores them without retraining by treating every skill as a trajectory that any tracker can run. It assigns each instruction the most precise of its best-validated frozen trackers, which ends each skill closer to the next one's start. It then builds each transition from the measured robot state, escalating to bridges and standing only when needed. On 400 instructions, CHOREO lifts sequence success to 95.8\% and beats always standing between skills by 2.8 points with 42\% shorter transitions. On a physical Unitree G1, all 45 zero-shot trials of nine five-action instructions succeed.
item.dc:creator: Ziyi Sun, Jingwen Chen, Yuxi Wang, Xiuze Xia, Long Cheng, Zhaoxiang Zhang, Junyu Dong

item.title: Connectivity-Aware Exploration of Robotic Grasp Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2609.22983v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robotic grasping is typically formulated as the problem of identifying successful actions from a space of candidate grasp poses. However, the organization of successful actions within this space has received less attention. We study the multiscale structure of viable robotic grasps in SE(3) and investigate whether this structure can be exploited for more efficient exploration. Using a large-scale grasp dataset, we show that successful grasp sets exhibit heterogeneous and reproducible connectivity structure across objects. We then introduce a connectivity-aware sampling strategy that incrementally explores the currently observed grasp space by prioritizing potential bridges between components, structural frontiers, boundary extensions, and geometric novelty. In controlled reconstruction experiments, the method recovers the connectivity structure of successful grasp sets substantially more efficiently than random sampling and farthest-point sampling. We further evaluate whether connectivity acquired under hidden grasp viability can improve subsequent grasp discovery, and whether structural experience from previously explored objects can be retrieved and transferred to unseen objects. These results suggest that the spatial organization of viable actions provides information relevant to grasp-space exploration beyond the viability of individual candidate actions. More broadly, they motivate structure-aware exploration as a means of exploiting the geometry of viable action spaces in robotic manipulation.
item.dc:creator: Maksim A Kazanskii

item.title: NEXUS: Perceptive Whole-Body Control for Terrain-Adaptive Teleoperation
item.description: arXiv:2609.39000v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whole-body teleoperation requires a humanoid robot to reproduce a human operator's behavior even when their terrains differ. This demands that the robot perceive local terrain and adapt its posture and contacts accordingly, rather than copy the operator's motion frame by frame. However, paired motion data linking the same behaviors across flat ground and different terrains remain scarce, limiting supervision for learning terrain-adaptive control. To enable whole-body teleoperation across mismatched terrains, we introduce NEXUS, a perceptive whole-body control framework that combines human motion commands with onboard sensory feedback. We first develop a scalable terrain-aware adaptation algorithm that efficiently generates high-quality motion pairs across motions and terrains without per-motion or per-terrain tuning. Using a paired motion corpus totaling nearly 1,000 hours, we train a perceptive whole-body controller through teacher-student learning to reproduce commanded behaviors across terrains. Experiments demonstrate efficient, scalable generation of high-quality motion data and show that NEXUS combines broad behavioral coverage with terrain adaptability and tracking fidelity, outperforming existing whole-body controllers on the evaluated benchmarks. Zero-shot real-world deployment enables real-time whole-body teleoperation on diverse unseen terrains, further validating the generalization of our method. Project website: https://nexus-humanoid.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Xiangyu Miao, Junsong Wu, Jiyuan Shi, Weiji Xie, Jinrui Han, Xingyi Wang, Weinan Zhang, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li

item.title: Visual Foresight for Agentic Reasoning Before Action in Urban Navigation
item.description: arXiv:2610.04916v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of action consequences, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, a training-free agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with visual foresight for reasoning before action. Our central idea is to use predicted future views to assess proposed actions in the context of persistent medium-horizon subgoals and observed experience. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. To enable visual foresight, a predictive world sandbox uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views of proposed movements, providing visual cues for reasoning about their consequences beyond the current observation. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions using the subgoal and accumulated experience to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
item.dc:creator: Jing Xie, Shouwei Ruan, Yubin Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Junwei Yang, Songchang Jin, Dianxi Shi

item.title: From Language to Motion: Task-Conditioned Focal-Stack Trajectory Integration for Microscopic Robots
item.description: arXiv:2610.12241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Microscopic visual servoing requires a robot to follow fine geometric features that a single image may reveal only in part. At high magnification, the field of view is limited, and shallow depth of field can leave different sections of the same contour sharp at different focal settings. These constraints also make training data costly to annotate, particularly when a change in part or task calls for a different edge, boundary, or offset path. We present a language-guided framework that addresses both the cost of configuring new tasks and the loss of usable geometry in any single focal plane. A language instruction specifies the geometry to recover, while frozen perception models and geometric operators locate it in the images. This separation enables zero-shot reconfiguration for the evaluated tasks without new task-specific training labels. To recover a path across focal planes, we extract local trajectories first and then select a consistent path from the segments supported by the image evidence. Each focal plane can thus contribute the sections it resolves well. The evaluated configuration took 15 minutes. Across nine part and illumination conditions, trajectory-level integration reduced 2-D contour RMSE by 56.4% relative to image-first fusion with SAMFF. In robot dispensing experiments, target-region coverage increased from 83.5% to 92.9%.
item.dc:creator: Junjie Xie, Chuxuan He, Junkai Huang, Heng Zhang, Angen Ye, Yujia Song, Yuqing Li, Pengsong Zhang, Dapeng Zhang

item.title: LiteNWM: Efficient Latent World Models for Onboard Visual Navigation in the Wild
item.description: arXiv:2610.12368v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Direct visual navigation policies generate trajectories efficiently but do not explicitly evaluate their future consequences. Generative navigation world models provide this foresight through visual rollouts, which are costly when evaluating multiple candidates. We present LiteNWM, a latent navigation world model that shares visual encoding across candidates and jointly predicts their action-conditioned future representations at multiple horizons, while a learned scorer uses these predictions to select trajectories. In offline evaluations on RECON, SCAND, and SACSoN, LiteNWM reduces macro-averaged trajectory error by 17.56% relative to NoMaD+NWM-XL and achieves a 128.00-fold end-to-end speedup on an RTX 5090. The same evaluator transfers from NoMaD to MBRA without proposer-specific retraining, reducing MBRA's macro-averaged trajectory error by 16.2%. In real-robot experiments in unseen indoor and outdoor environments, LiteNWM improves navigation success from 43.3% to 83.3% relative to NoMaD. These results demonstrate that LiteNWM can be deployed for future-aware planning and closed-loop navigation on a physical robot.
item.dc:creator: Linkai Liu, Yuntian Zhang, Zhenshan Bing, Chen Chen, Lingjuan Lyu, Shangguang Wang, Mengwei Xu, Dongqi Cai

item.title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.21522v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
item.dc:creator: Lichao Ni, Yuhan Liu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang

item.title: Safe Task Completion via Graph-Based Planning for LLM-Powered Robots
item.description: arXiv:2610.24603v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are used to drive robotic manipulation and planning, yet deploying them on physical systems exposes risks, including jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mostly evaluated on short instructions with a single hazard. Real tasks may mix safe and unsafe sub-tasks, or combine individually safe actions into an unsafe outcome. For such compound instructions, a single safety decision either misses the hazard or rejects the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-powered robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules framework that verifies safety at multiple stages rather than relying on a single one. Five agents ground safety principles into world-specific rules, judge each sub-task in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is organized as a graph in which each node handles its assigned rules. Candidate plans are verified and aggregated level by level until one plan satisfies every rule. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions from two benchmarks, measuring Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reaches 0% ASR on both benchmarks and highest TSR among all methods, with 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 83.51% on our long-horizon compound instructions.
item.dc:creator: Ali Taheri, Alireza Taban, Qizhou Wang, Wanhua Li

item.title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.25600v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere

item.title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.28164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoxu Xu, Hao Li, Hongtao Zhang, Yili Tang, Jiafei Cao, Junhao Cai, Haoxiang Ma, Weixin Li, Weinan Zhang

item.title: MyoAcross: A Framework for Scalable Individualized Musculoskeletal Simulation with a Generalist Morphology-Conditioned Policy
item.description: arXiv:2610.36535v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Musculoskeletal simulations powered by deep reinforcement learning (DRL) support human-robot interaction design and rehabilitation engineering, and they typically rely on a generic template model. However, differences in skeletal proportions and body mass alter dynamics, limiting the fidelity of generic models and the reuse of policies trained on them. Scaling individualized simulations requires a framework that connects model construction from accessible inputs with a generalist policy that transfers without fine-tuning. We present MyoAcross, which integrates skeletal-guided individual model construction, generalist morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation for full-body muscle-driven control. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion with a 53.70 mm tracking error, compared with 8.32% completion for a baseline policy trained only on the generic model. Ablation studies show that morphology conditioning improves tracking accuracy while virtual model augmentation broadens generalization. Across input modalities, the pretrained policy demonstrates generalizability to models constructed from body shape (paired with mass), monocular images (paired with height and mass), and marker-based motion capture (paired with mass), making MyoAcross scalable. For biomechanical assessment, MyoAcross improves agreement with measured ground reaction forces and surface electromyography over the generic model on the external Gait120 dataset. These results establish MyoAcross as a practical framework for scalable individualized musculoskeletal simulation. It is suited for systematic cross-individual applications, such as exoskeleton DRL assistance policy design.
item.dc:creator: Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang, Yiheng He, Xinjun Liu, Senhao Hou, Huichan Zhao, Xiaoqiang Tang

item.title: A Bi-level Co-design Framework for Lunar Monoped with 2D Jump and Landing Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.37199v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Legged robots for lunar exploration must be designed for low gravity, where reduced contact forces and long flight phases make leg morphology and controller choice interdependent. We study this for a planar monoped in lunar gravity (1.625 m/s^2) using a bi-level co-design framework: a differential evolution outer loop searches over link lengths, and each candidate is evaluated on a vertical jump by either a quadratic program based task-space controller (QP-TSC) or a direct-collocation based trajectory optimization. The two controllers yield different optimal link lengths, and trajectory optimization outperforms the QP-TSC across most of the design space, with 17% lower Cost of Transport (COT) at their respective optima. We then extend to a 2D jump, where trajectory optimization with centroidal angular momentum regulation produces stable in-place and forward jumps, and an LQR controller absorbs impact and stabilizes the robot after touchdown. This is demonstrated on a baseline morphology with both links 0.3 m long.
item.dc:creator: Sanjay Ramkumar, Suraj Kumar

item.title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2610.41857v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulation benchmarks score robot policies by success rate, and every failed episode counts against the policy. Testing over ten vision language action and world action models on five benchmarks, we find that failures in which the policy has placed the object and the simulator then throws it out are frequent, and that the benchmark's own scripted demonstrations fail the same way. We present SimuGuard, an auditing plugin for LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa, RoboDojo and RoboLab. At every physics step, it records the state and flags an object that starts moving at a contact faster than the robot's contact or gravity account for. It replays a recorded episode bit for bit, and it reruns the episode with one solver parameter changed. With it we trace each such episode to a false contact. A fixed threshold in PhysX's collision detection makes the engine report an overlap of about two centimeters between the placed object and the thin wall of its container, where the two do not touch. The solver removes the whole overlap in one step and throws the object out at several meters per second. With a smaller threshold, LingBot-VA succeeds in 98 of 100 new episodes against 89, and no episode has an artifact. Across five models, the ranking in the repaired engine follows the ranking on a real robot. SimuGuard also finds two other simulation errors: objects that start inside their support, and objects stuck to an open gripper. SimuGuard lets a benchmark separate what the policy did from what the solver did.
item.dc:creator: Alex Zhou, Junhao Wu, Xueyang Zhou, Yixiao Huo, Hongcheng Gao, Di Zhu, Zhenghao Zhang, Yongchao Chen

item.title: Positive Safety Margins from Artificial Potential Field Reward Augmentation for Size-Robust Obstacle Avoidance under Partial Observability
item.description: arXiv:2611.02947v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy.
